extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: SciQ is a dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a novel two-step method. The method leverages a large corpus of domain-specific science textbooks and a small set of existing questions, using model suggestions for document selection and answer distractor choice to aid human question generation. Each instance consists of a question, four answer options, and an associated passage used to formulate the question. The dataset covers biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics topics spanning elementary to college introductory level.
extraction.license: Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial 3.0 Unported (CC BY-NC 3.0) for CK-12 books; Creative Commons License for OpenStax materials
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Welbl, J., Liu, N. F., & Gardner, M. (2017). Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209v1 [cs.HC].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through a two-step crowdsourcing process on Amazon Mechanical Turk. In the first step, crowd workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one, and formulated a question answerable from the passage. In the second step, another worker validated the question and selected or wrote answer distractors, aided by model-generated distractor suggestions. A total of 175 workers participated. The total budget was $10,415.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In 12.1% of cases, all three presented documents were rejected by crowd workers as irrelevant. A small percentage of passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller (10,481 train, 887 dev, 884 test) compared to the multiple choice version.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Science study textbooks from 28 books compiled from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics from elementary to college introductory level. A set of 3,705 real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions was used to train the distractor model.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was randomly shuffled and split into training, validation, and test portions, with 1,000 questions each in validation and test, and the remainder in training. A direct-answer version was also created using the associated passage and question without answer options, excluding passages from unreleasable texts.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to individual paragraphs of the base corpus. Sentences were filtered out if they: were questions or exclamations, had no verb phrase, contained modal verbs, contained imperative phrases, contained demonstrative pronouns, contained personal pronouns other than third-person, began with a pronoun, contained first names, had fewer than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas, contained special characters other than punctuation, had more than three tokens beginning uppercase, mentioned a graph/table/web link, began with a discourse marker, contained absolute wording, or contained instructional vocabulary. A paragraph was accepted if a minimum number of sentences passed the filter.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step crowdsourcing annotation: (1) Question Formulation Task: Workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one, and wrote a question answerable from the passage. Guidelines specified no yes/no questions, questions querying general principles, question length 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguous questions. Workers were paid $0.30 per HIT. (2) Distractor Selection Task: Workers validated the question (marking it as ungrammatical, having a false answer, unrelated to science, or requiring very specific background knowledge), selected up to two of six model-suggested distractors, and wrote at least one distractor themselves. Workers were paid $0.20 per HIT. AMT Master's status was required for both tasks.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: 92.8% of questions passed the quality control validation in the distractor selection task. On average, crowd workers found the predicted distractors good enough to include about half the time, resulting in 36.1% of distractors in the final dataset being model-generated. A qualitative evaluation showed that humans could only identify the real science exam question over the crowdsourced question in 55% of cases, which falls below the significance level of p=0.05 under a null hypothesis of random guessing.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question has one correct answer and three distractors. The distractor selection task involved one worker per question for validation and distractor selection/generation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A total of 175 workers participated in the crowdsourcing project. AMT Master's status was required for all workers. No further demographic information is provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A random forest classifier trained on 3,705 real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions was used to suggest answer distractors. Features included GloVe embeddings, POS-tag consistency indicators, WordNet-based hypernymy indicators, OpenIE-based knowledge base links from Simple Wikipedia, and various lexical and morphological features. The candidate distractor set contained 488,819 expressions including GloVe vocabulary, observed distractors, noun phrases from Simple Wikipedia, and noun vocabulary from primary school science texts. Scikit-learn's random forest implementation with 500 trees was used.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is released for future research at http://allenai.org/data.html. No explicit versioning, update schedule, or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance science exam question answering, a high-level NLP task requiring information extraction, reading comprehension, and common sense reasoning. It addresses the bottleneck of limited in-domain training data for science QA, potentially enabling better educational AI systems.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The base corpus is limited to 28 science study textbooks from specific online learning resources (CK-12 and OpenStax), which may not represent the full diversity of science education materials. The distractor model was trained on 4th and 8th grade science exam questions, which may bias distractor suggestions toward those grade levels.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is domain-specific to science questions at elementary to college introductory level. Neural models do not outperform simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version, suggesting limitations for studying neural reading comprehension. The direct answer version is smaller due to unreleasable source texts. Multiword expression distractors were more likely to be unrelated or ungrammatical. The distractor model quality is not high enough to use predictions directly without human filtering.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of science exam question answering systems. The dataset supports both a multiple choice setting (selecting correct answer from options without the passage) and a direct answer setting (predicting answer span given passage and question). It can be used as additional training data to improve performance on real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions. Useful for studying neural model performance in medium-sized data settings (tens of thousands of examples).
